251.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, the dinner of beans and rice is excellent, if it is flavored with salt. Who would cut his throat, to have meat with his bread?”
251.explanation: In his saloks preserved in the Guru Granth Sahib, Bhagat Kabir says a plain meal of khichri and salt is good food, and asks who would slit a throat just to have meat with his bread.
251.tie_back: The Kural condemns taking another creature's flesh to fatten one's own body; Kabir sets the same choice before the eater, simple food against a life taken for the sake of the palate.
251.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1374, Salok Bhagat Kabir 188 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
251._accuracy_note: Strong thematic fit on killing for one's appetite, but the salok is set against ritual slaughter and Sikh teaching does not read it as a universal ban on meat, so it is not a full match for the Kural's position.

252.quote_or_event: “You say that the One Lord is in all, so why do you kill chickens?”
252.explanation: In a hymn in Raag Prabhaatee, Kabir challenges a cleric: if he truly believes God lives in every creature, killing one goes against his own faith.
252.tie_back: Valluvar says a flesh-eater cannot hold on to the wealth of compassion; Kabir says that killing empties out the very belief in God's presence in every life that compassion rests on.
252.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1350, Raag Prabhaatee, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
252._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit: both say killing contradicts a professed inner virtue, but Kabir's target is ritual sacrifice by a cleric, and the Kural's comparison with guarding wealth has no parallel here.

253.quote_or_event: “If one's clothes are stained with blood, the garment becomes polluted. Those who suck the blood of human beings-how can their consciousness be pure?”
253.explanation: In a salok of Vaar Maajh, Guru Nanak points out that people call a bloodstained garment impure, and asks how the mind of someone who lives off other people's blood can ever be clean.
253.tie_back: The Kural says a mind that has relished another body cannot turn toward goodness, like the mind of one holding a weapon; Guru Nanak likewise holds that feeding on others' blood leaves the consciousness impure.
253.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 140, Vaar Maajh (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
253._accuracy_note: Partial: the image of a mind defiled by living off others' blood matches well, but Guru Nanak's blood-drinkers are exploiters of people, not meat-eaters.

254.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, they oppress living beings and kill them, and call it proper. When the Lord calls for their account, what will their condition be?”
254.explanation: Kabir rejects the claim that killing a creature by force becomes acceptable because it is labelled proper, and warns that God will call such killers to account.
254.tie_back: The Kural flatly calls killing the opposite of grace and says eating what was killed is not right; Kabir likewise refuses to let any label turn killing into righteousness.
254.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1375, Salok Bhagat Kabir 199 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
254._accuracy_note: Strong fit on killing as wrong no matter what it is called, but Kabir's specific target is ritual 'halal' slaughter and he does not define compassion as non-killing in the Kural's catechism form.

255.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, those mortals who consume marijuana, fish and wine - no matter what pilgrimages, fasts and rituals they follow, they will all go to hell.”
255.explanation: Kabir warns that people who eat fish and take intoxicants are not saved by their pilgrimages, fasts or rituals, but go down to hell.
255.tie_back: Valluvar says hell swallows the flesh-eater and does not let him go; Kabir's salok also sends the eater of flesh to hell, whatever religious merit he claims.
255.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1377, Salok Bhagat Kabir 233 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
255._accuracy_note: Strong fit on the hellward fate of the flesh-eater, though Kabir groups fish with intoxicants, and some Sikh commentators (e.g. Sahib Singh) read 'rasaatal' as the rituals going to waste rather than literal hell.

256.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, it is tyranny to use force; the Lord shall call you to account.”
256.explanation: Kabir says that any use of force against another living being is oppression, and God will demand an answer for it.
256.tie_back: Valluvar refuses to let the buyer of meat shift the blame to the butcher; the nearest Sikh teaching is that everyone who takes part in violence answers for it.
256.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1375, Salok Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
256._accuracy_note: Next-best only: Gurbani has no equivalent of the Kural's economic argument that demand creates the killing; this verse only makes violence accountable.

257.quote_or_event: “You seize a living creature, and then bring it home and kill its body; you have killed only the clay.”
257.explanation: Kabir strips away the religious language around ritual slaughter and describes what actually happens: a living creature is caught and its body destroyed, and he adds that this 'offering' gains the slayer nothing.
257.tie_back: Valluvar makes people see meat for what it is, another creature's wound; Kabir similarly describes the slaughter in plain words so it can no longer be dressed up as piety.
257.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1350, Raag Prabhaatee, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
257._accuracy_note: Partial: both describe the killing in plain terms to expose it, but Kabir's 'only the clay' points to the soul surviving and to the uselessness of sacrifice, not to the creature's suffering as the Kural's 'wound' does.

258.quote_or_event: “The fools argue about flesh and meat, but they know nothing about meditation and spiritual wisdom. What is called meat, and what is called green vegetables? What leads to sin?”
258.explanation: In Vaar Malaar Guru Nanak mocks those who make meat-eating the test of holiness while knowing nothing of meditation or spiritual wisdom.
258.tie_back: The Kural says those whose vision is free of delusion will not eat flesh; Guru Nanak agrees that clear vision is what matters but places it in spiritual wisdom, not in avoiding meat.
258.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1289, Vaar Malaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
258._accuracy_note: Honest contrast rather than parallel: Guru Nanak refuses to make diet the measure of wisdom, which runs against this Kural, and Sikh opinion on meat-eating remains divided.

259.quote_or_event: “You kill living beings, and call it a righteous action. Tell me, brother, what would you call an unrighteous action?”
259.explanation: In Raag Maaroo Kabir asks a priest who kills animals in sacrificial rites how he can call that dharma, and what then he would call sin.
259.tie_back: Valluvar ranks not killing a single creature above a thousand fire-sacrifices; Kabir likewise rejects killing done in the name of sacred rites.
259.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1103, Raag Maaroo, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
259._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: both judge sacrificial killing against the plain ethics of not killing; traditional commentators (Faridkot Teeka, Sahib Singh) read the line as aimed at yajna sacrifice.

260.quote_or_event: “And when, O Nanak, he is merciful to all beings, only then shall he be called a Muslim.”
260.explanation: In a salok of Vaar Maajh Guru Nanak lists the real marks of a believer and ends by saying that only someone merciful to all living beings has earned the name.
260.tie_back: The Kural promises the reverence of all living beings to the one who neither kills nor eats flesh; Guru Nanak likewise makes mercy toward all beings the condition for true religious honour.
260.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 141, Vaar Maajh (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
260._accuracy_note: Next-best: mercy to all beings matches the Kural's condition, but the verse is addressed to Muslims, says nothing of meat, and has no image of all creatures worshipping.
